title: Explore
intro: Walk through a museum of antimicrobial resistance: the proteins bacteria use to survive our medicine, the research that tracks them, and a shooting gallery where you are in charge of the antibiotics.
controls_desktop: Click and drag to look · WASD to walk · Q/E to turn · H for help · Esc for menu
controls_touch: Left thumb to walk · drag on the right to look · tap the speech bubble
sign_welcome_sub: Rare Microbe Bioinformatics Lab (RaMBio) · DTU National Food Institute
desc.1BTL: The first beta-lactamase found on a plasmid, in 1965. A pair of molecular scissors that cuts the ring at the heart of penicillin.
desc.4HBT: The world's most widespread extended-spectrum beta-lactamase. It cuts modern cephalosporins such as cefotaxime.
desc.2OV5: A carbapenemase that broke through one of our last lines of defence and spread across the globe in Klebsiella.
desc.3SPU: Named after New Delhi. A metallo-beta-lactamase that grips zinc ions to tear apart almost every beta-lactam.
desc.3HBR: First found in Turkey in 2001, now common across Europe. Two copies work together as a pair.
desc.1V0C: Sticks a small acetyl tag onto aminoglycosides like amikacin, so they no longer fit their target on the ribosome. Captured here with kanamycin bound.
desc.1VQQ: The reason MRSA exists. A spare cell-wall builder that penicillin-like drugs can barely grab.
desc.1E4E: Rebuilds the cell wall's anchor so vancomycin loses its grip, around a thousand times weaker binding.
desc.5LRN: Discovered in Chinese pigs in 2015: the first mobile colistin resistance gene. It decorates the outer membrane so colistin slides off. Shown: the catalytic domain.
desc.2GIF: A three-part pump in the inner membrane. Each subunit cycles through loose, tight and open states, pushing many drugs out of the cell.
mascot.0: Hi there! Welcome to Explore, a museum about antimicrobial resistance. I'm a rod-shaped gut bacterium, a kind of E. coli.
mascot.1: Straight ahead is the protein gallery: ten proteins that help bacteria like me survive antibiotics. Today's protein from PanRes spins right here in the middle of the hall.
mascot.2: To the right is our research. To the left is the shooting gallery, where you fight infections with antibiotics. And behind you, the learning room shows films about microbes.
mascot.3: Some proteins cut the antibiotic to pieces, some change the spot it is meant to hit, and some simply pump it back out. Have fun exploring!

game_sub: How long will the medicine last?
game_prompt: Press Space to step up to the counter
game_intro:
Shoot the disease-causing bacteria (+10 per cell) and spare the friendly ones (−15 per cell). The board on the counter shows who is who: the colour is the Gram stain, and the shape tells you the species.
Tablets (rifle) are narrow-spectrum: penicillin and vancomycin only kill Gram-positives (purple), gentamicin and colistin only Gram-negatives (pink). One tablet kills one cell. The imipenem capsule (shotgun) is broad-spectrum: it wipes out whole clusters, friends included.
Watch the knobs on the bacteria: they are resistance proteins in the colour of the drug they defeat. Switch drugs with 1–5, the mouse wheel or the buttons.
rainbow_hint: The colours follow the protein chain: from blue at the start to red at the end.
research_inst: DTU National Food Institute · Technical University of Denmark
research_p1: We read the DNA of entire microbial communities, from sewage, animals and people, without having to grow a single bacterium.
research_p2: With sewage from more than 100 countries, we map which resistance genes travel where, and which bacteria carry them.
research_p3: We build open tools for everyone: the PanRes database of resistance genes, Flankophile for the genes’ neighbours in the DNA, and MGCalibrator for counting microbes in absolute numbers.
edu_sub: Short films from RaMBio, and where to go next
link_stopamr: A Danish website about antimicrobial resistance and how we can slow it down.
link_alliancen: Patient groups, researchers, hospitals, unions and the life-science industry together, for a future where every resistant infection can be cured.
pw_structures_sub: AlphaFold models of the protein families
pw_classes_sub: from beta-lactams to metals and disinfectants
game_legend_bugs: Who's who? The colour is the Gram stain, the shape is the species
game_legend_drugs: Your drugs · knobs in the same colour = resistance
game_phase0: Every drug still works. Choose the narrow one that fits.
game_phase1: Blue knobs: MRSA’s PBP2a shrugs off penicillin, so use vancomycin. Yellow knobs: AAC(6′)-Ib destroys gentamicin, so use colistin.
game_phase2: Orange knobs: VanA defeats vancomycin. Teal knobs: MCR-1 defeats colistin. When the tablets fail, only the broad capsule is left.
game_phase3: Red knobs: KPC and NDM-1 break down imipenem. Now the capsule fails too, so find the tablet that still works.
game_phase4: Bacteria with knobs of every colour pour in. Nothing in your arsenal works any more.
game_over_body:
The last bacteria were resistant to every drug you had. That is called pan-resistance, and it already exists: some hospital infections today cannot be cured with any antibiotic.
Each knob was a real resistance protein, and you can see several of them up close in the protein gallery. The less we use antibiotics, and the more precisely we use them, the more slowly resistance spreads.
